Why trustworthy and responsible AI?

AI systems now help decide who gets a loan, which medical scan gets a second look, and what information millions of people see every day. When these systems are biased, opaque, brittle or misaligned with human values, the harm is real and falls hardest on those least able to contest it. Trustworthy and responsible AI (TRAI) is the effort to make sure AI is fair to the people it affects, protects their privacy, can explain its decisions, stays robust when conditions change or an adversary intervenes, and remains aligned with the intentions and norms of the people it serves. These properties are not add-ons: they have to be measured, designed and verified with the same rigour as accuracy. The Trustworthy and Responsible AI Lab (TRAIL) at METU brings together four research groups working on these questions, from theory to applications in computer vision, affective computing, multi-agent systems and scientific machine learning.

What we have contributed

  • Emre Akbaş works on concept-based explainability: rethinking concept bottleneck models and fixing their pitfalls, explaining the zero-shot predictions of CLIP through human-understandable concepts, caption bottleneck models, and benchmarks for evaluating concept-based explanations. His group also studies out-of-distribution detection and data imbalance in face recognition.
  • Hüseyin Aydın studies privacy and cooperation in multi-agent and human-AI systems: multi-agent reinforcement learning and computational theory of mind for resolving users’ privacy conflicts, privacy dynamics in groups, fairness-aware incentives in sequential social dilemmas, and frameworks for human-AI interaction experiments.
  • Gökberk Cinbiş works on robustness and privacy of learning systems: the adversarial robustness of zero-shot learning models, frequency-based data augmentation for model robustness (HybridAugment++), privacy-preserving collaborative learning, and reward-based tuning of generative image models.
  • Sinan Kalkan works on fairness and explainability: bias and fairness in facial affect recognition and mental-health prediction (counterfactual and causal fairness, uncertainty as a fairness measure, fair multimodal self-supervised learning), quantitative and verbalised analysis of explanation heatmaps, explainable machine learning for scientific forecasting, disentangled representations, and adversarial robustness in object detection.

See the Research page for our themes and the Publications page for the full list of papers.
